dinosaur: a kind of reptile that ruled the land long ago
reptile: a scaly cold-blooded animal, like a lizard or crocodile
fossil: the remains of a living thing turned to stone
palaeontologist: a scientist who studies fossils
asteroid: a large lump of rock travelling through space
descendant: a living thing that comes from an earlier kind

Long before there were any people, before there were even any cats or dogs or cows, the Earth belonged to other creatures entirely. For over a hundred and fifty million years, the land shook under the feet of the dinosaurs. That is a stretch of time so long that the human story beside it is barely a blink.

image.note: A prehistoric landscape, no people anywhere, giant dinosaurs among huge ferns; ancient, wild

pages.text: The world back then would look strange to you. There was no grass at all, for grass had not yet appeared. Ferns and giant tree-like plants covered the land. The very shape of the continents was different, once all joined in a single huge landmass before slowly drifting apart. It was Earth, but not as you know it.

image.note: The single ancient supercontinent shown, then beginning to split; a world map that looks wrong

pages.text: So what actually was a dinosaur? Dinosaurs were reptiles, cousins of today's lizards and crocodiles, but with a difference that set them apart. Their legs grew straight down beneath their bodies, like a dog or a horse, instead of sprawling out to the sides like a lizard. That let them stand tall, run fast, and grow truly enormous.

image.note: A diagram comparing a sprawling lizard with an upright dinosaur leg posture; clear, simple

pages.text: There was no single kind of dinosaur. There were hundreds and hundreds of kinds, over the ages, in every shape you can imagine. Some were smaller than a chicken. Some were longer than three buses in a row. Some ate only plants, some ate only meat, and each had its own place in that long-vanished world.

image.note: A size line-up: a tiny chicken-sized dinosaur beside a towering long-necked one; scale

pages.text: The largest dinosaurs were the long-necked plant-eaters, the biggest animals ever to walk the Earth. With necks like cranes, they could reach the freshest leaves at the very tops of the tallest trees, where nothing else could feed. They spent almost all day eating, for a body that size took a mountain of leaves to fill.

image.note: A vast long-necked dinosaur reaching into treetops, tiny others grazing below; grand scale

pages.text: These giants were not fighters. They were gentle grazers, and their great size was their shield, for few hunters would dare attack something so huge. Some had long whip-like tails they could crack for defence. Others were armoured with bony plates and clubbed tails, walking tanks that even the fiercest hunter thought twice about.

image.note: An armoured, club-tailed dinosaur standing firm; a predator hesitating nearby; standoff

pages.text: Where there are plant-eaters, there are hunters. The meat-eating dinosaurs walked on two legs, freeing their clawed hands to grip, and their jaws were lined with teeth like knives. The most famous of all was Tyrannosaurus, taller than a house, with a bite powerful enough to crush bone.

image.note: A large two-legged predator mid-stride, jaws open, small arms; powerful, not gory

pages.text: But bigness was not the only way to hunt. Some smaller meat-eaters were swift and clever, and hunted together in packs, the way wild dogs do today. Working as a team, they could bring down prey far larger than any of them alone. The old idea that dinosaurs were slow and stupid has turned out to be quite wrong.

image.note: A pack of small swift dinosaurs coordinating a hunt; alert, intelligent-looking; no blood

pages.text: Here is the puzzle. No human ever saw a living dinosaur. So how do we know any of this? The answer lies buried in the rock. When a dinosaur died and was quickly covered by mud or sand, its bones could slowly turn to stone over millions of years. These stony bones are called fossils.

image.note: A dinosaur bone half-buried in rock layers; a fossil forming over deep time; cross-section

pages.text: Scientists called palaeontologists dig these fossils up with tiny brushes and great patience. From a skeleton in the ground they can work out how big the animal was, how it moved, and what it ate from the shape of its teeth. Every fossil is a message written in bone, sent to us across a hundred million years.

image.note: Palaeontologists carefully brushing a large fossil skeleton out of the ground; painstaking, exciting

pages.text: For all their power, the age of the dinosaurs ended, and it ended suddenly. About sixty-six million years ago, a mountain of rock from space, an asteroid, struck the Earth with unimaginable force. It threw up so much dust that the sky darkened across the whole planet for a very long time.

image.note: A great asteroid streaking down toward a distant Earth; dinosaurs looking up; dramatic, not graphic

pages.text: With the sky darkened, the plants could not grow. With the plants gone, the plant-eaters starved, and then the hunters that fed on them starved too. In a short time, all the great dinosaurs were gone. An age that had lasted over a hundred million years was over. The world had to begin again.

image.note: A dim, dust-veiled world with withered ferns; empty of dinosaurs; quiet, sombre, not gruesome

pages.text: And yet, this is not quite a story of ending. Some small, feathered dinosaurs survived that terrible time. Over millions of years, their children changed, and changed again, and became something you see every single day. The birds in the sky above your head are the living descendants of the dinosaurs.

image.note: A small feathered dinosaur beside a modern bird, one clearly becoming the other; surprising, warm

pages.text: So the dinosaurs never fully died out. When a chicken struts across a yard, when a hawk circles overhead, a distant echo of that ancient age is passing before your eyes. Look at a bird's scaly feet and sharp eye, and you are looking at the last of the dinosaurs, still walking among us.

image.note: A hawk circling over a modern Nigerian estate, its shadow like a tiny dinosaur; a child watching, closing
